title: Just How Rosy Is That Datacenter Buildout Forecast?
gist: Jeffries, with Aterio data, forecasts that North American datacenter capacity additions will fall far short of hyperscaler plans because labor, cooling equipment and power constrain buildouts, with expected hyperscaler builds falling to 4.46 GW in 2030 versus 13.82 GW planned. Meanwhile US Census data shows datacenter and utility construction offsetting declines in commercial and residential construction.

themes.theme: Physical constraints cap the GenAI buildout

insights.claim: The GenAI boom can only grow as fast as datacenters are built and powered, and no amount of money or political pressure can speed up installation of power generation equipment.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Capital spending alone does not translate into AI capacity; physical bottlenecks set the pace.
insights.quote: No amount of political, social, or economic pressure can speed up how power generation equipment is installed at datacenters or at utilities.

insights.claim: Supply chains from chip manufacturing equipment to chip makers to power distribution equipment makers were not ready to ramp as quickly as the AI boom requires.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Suppliers of grid and electrical equipment face demand outstripping their capacity to ramp.

insights.claim: Jeffries' Jonathan Petersen argues that grid interconnects, hyperscaler capex, or chip sales projections in isolation miss the picture: bringing datacenter capacity online requires all of those plus labor, electrical and cooling equipment manufacturing, and a cooperative political and regulatory environment.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Tracking capex or chip sales alone will overestimate the real datacenter capacity coming online.

insights.claim: According to Jeffries, labor is the biggest constraint on datacenter spending in 2026, cooling equipment is the main constraint from 2027 through 2029, and available power becomes the main constraint in 2030.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Identifies which bottleneck (labor, cooling, power) will bind in each year, pointing to where pricing power may shift.
insights.quote: In 2026, labor is the biggest damper on datacenter spending, and in 2027 through 2029, it will be cooling equipment. In 2030, the main constraint will be available power, says Jeffries.

themes.theme: Datacenter construction propping up the US economy

insights.claim: US construction data through August 2026, charted by Harvard economist Jason Furman, shows datacenter and power utility construction growth counter-balancing declines in commercial and residential construction.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: US construction activity is increasingly dependent on the AI datacenter cycle, a macro risk if it slows.
insights.quote: datacenter capacity construction increases, and to a certain extent for power utilities as well, are counter-balancing the declines seen in commercial and residential construction in the United States

insights.claim: High mortgage interest rates conveniently free up construction labor for datacenter projects at a time when builders want more workers on datacenters rather than homes or offices.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Weak housing construction may be easing the labor bottleneck for datacenter builds.

insights.so_what: Confirms the scale and acceleration of private datacenter construction spending since the GenAI inflection.

themes.theme: Jeffries/Aterio forecast: planned vs. buildable capacity

insights.claim: Jeffries tracks about 65 IT gigawatts of North American datacenters under construction (about 140 percent of installed capacity) and another roughly 361 GW of announced future projects (about 760 percent), but expects many to be delayed or canceled.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: The announced pipeline vastly exceeds what can realistically be delivered, so headline project counts overstate supply.
insights.quote: Our dataset tracks ~65 IT GW of DCs under construction (~140 percent of installed capacity), and another ~361 GW of future announced projects (~760 percent).
insights.locator: The AI industry has a datacenter problem

insights.claim: Jeffries expects 12.9 GW of new North American datacenter IT capacity in 2026 and 18 GW in 2027, with demand for inference and frontier model training growing faster than capacity can come online.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Capacity scarcity supports pricing for those who already hold powered datacenter capacity.
insights.quote: We expect 12.9 GWs of new capacity in 2026 and 18 GWs in 2027.

insights.claim: Jeffries' bear case is driven by labor shortages, political pressure for datacenters to pay their share of electricity generation costs, and community skepticism about local benefits, while even the bull case assumes many delays and some cancellations.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Political and community pushback is a growing risk factor for datacenter developers and power-cost allocation.

insights.claim: Jeffries expects North American hyperscalers to build only 7.53 GW versus 8.37 GW planned in 2027, 6.54 GW versus 10.13 GW in 2028, 5.86 GW versus just under 18 GW in 2029, and 4.46 GW versus 13.82 GW in 2030, with 2026 converging at 6.21 GW.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Even cash-rich hyperscalers face widening shortfalls, implying capex may be deferred and buildout falls short of plans.

insights.claim: Even hyperscalers with very strong balance sheets will not be able to build datacenters at the rate they want, and Jeffries' expected completed capacity declines each year from 2027 through 2030.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Bullish AI infrastructure forecasts based on hyperscaler plans are likely too rosy.
